title: Statistics and probability
text: Probability is a calculus of uncertainty with a measure underneath. Statistics is the inverse problem: data in, statements about a mechanism out. This page keeps the two in one place so the vocabulary stays aligned.

title: Statistics and probability
text:
1 Probability, as a machine
A probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is the stage. A random variable is a measurable map \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) (or \(\mathbb R^d\)). The law of \(X\) is the push-forward \(\mathbb P\circ X^{-1}\).
Working objects:

Expectation \(\mathbb E[X]\) as an integral; linearity does not need independence.
Variance as the \(L^2\) distance to the mean.
Independence as factorisation of joint laws (or of \(\sigma\)-algebras).
Conditioning as “restrict, then renormalise”: \(\mathbb P(A\mid B) = \mathbb P(A\cap B)/\mathbb P(B)\) when \(\mathbb P(B)>0\), and the conditional-expectation version when \(B\) is a \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Bayes’ theorem is that last idea written for a parameter and a likelihood.

title: Statistics and probability
text:
2 The usual limit theorems
Three statements do most of the daily work.

Law of large numbers. Sample means converge (in probability, or almost surely) to \(\mathbb E[X]\) when the mean exists.
Central limit theorem. Fluctuations of the mean, after \(\sqrt n\) scaling, become Gaussian under a second-moment hypothesis.
Concentration. Tail bounds (Hoeffding, Bernstein, …) when you need finite-\(n\) control, not only an asymptotic shape.

These are analysis theorems about measures. The analysis page is where characteristic functions and inversion live.

title: Statistics and probability
text:
3 Statistics, as inverse probability
A model is a family of laws \(\{P_\theta\}\). Data \(x\) is treated as a realisation of \(X\sim P_\theta\). Standard jobs:



Job
Typical object




Point estimate
MLE, method of moments, Bayes posterior mean


Interval
Confidence set or credible set


Test
\(H_0\) versus \(H_1\); \(p\)-value as a tail of a null


Prediction
A law for a new \(X\), not only for \(\theta\)



Linear models later reuse matrix decompositions (QR for least squares, SVD for PCA, Cholesky for covariances).

title: Statistics and probability
text:
4 Dynamic modelling
Markov chains are the simplest dynamics with noise: the next state depends on the present, not on the path that got you there. They are classified by time (discrete or continuous), by the size of the state space, by transition structure (absorbing, irreducible, ergodic), and by whether the state is observed. The types overlap: a discrete-time chain can also be finite and absorbing. Hidden Markov models keep the chain latent and emit observations.

title: Linear algebra

1 Introduction to vectors
A vector is an element of a vector space: you can add two and scale one, and you stay in the space. Arrows in the plane are the first picture, not the definition. Functions, polynomials, and matrices can be vectors too.

title: Linear algebra
text:
3 Methods of matrix inversion
There is no single best inverse. Gauss–Jordan is pedagogical; adjugate is for small symbolic work; LU, QR, Cholesky, and SVD are the numerical defaults. Forming \(A^{-1}\) is often the wrong move: solve \(Ax=b\) with a factorisation instead.

title: Linear algebra
text:
4 Eigenvalue algorithms
\(A v = \lambda v\) is the decomposition \(A = X\Lambda X^{-1}\) when \(A\) is diagonalisable. Which algorithm you want depends on whether \(A\) is sparse or symmetric, and on whether you need one eigenpair or the whole spectrum. Do not form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) as a numerical primitive.
6 September 2026.






Eigenvalue algorithms: match the method to the matrix.

title: Differential equations
text:
A differential equation is a constraint on a function and its derivatives. In mechanics that function is a trajectory. The same curve can be written as a second-order ODE in position, as a stationary-action problem, as a first-order flow on phase space, or as a first-order nonlinear PDE for a generating function.
This page is a map, not a textbook. Two galleries from @eeanimation carry the pictures: a tour of dynamical-systems language, then four equivalent formulations of classical motion.

title: Differential equations
text:
1 Topics of dynamical systems
Continuous time is \(\dot x = f(x,t)\). Discrete time is \(x_{k+1} = F(x_k)\). The same vocabulary — equilibria, linearisation, Lyapunov functions, bifurcations, Poincaré maps, chaos — asks whether trajectories converge, oscillate, or become sensitive to the initial state.

\(\sum \mathbf F = m\ddot{\mathbf r}\)


Lagrangian

When the modelling assumptions match (holonomic constraints, a regular Lagrangian, forces that the chosen language can express), these formulations predict the same classical trajectories. They do not emphasise the same structure.

title: Differential equations
text:
3 Worked motif: the simple pendulum
A mass \(m\) on a massless rod of length \(\ell\), angle \(\theta\) from the downward vertical. One generalised coordinate is enough.
Newtonian (tangential balance):
\[
\ddot\theta + \frac{g}{\ell}\sin\theta = 0.
\]
Lagrangian \(L = T - V\) with \(T = \tfrac12 m\ell^2\dot\theta^2\) and \(V = mg\ell(1-\cos\theta)\) yields the same ODE from the Euler–Lagrange equation. The Hamiltonian picture replaces \(\dot\theta\) by \(p_\theta = \partial L/\partial\dot\theta\) and reads the motion as a curve in the \((\theta,p_\theta)\) plane.

title: Differential equations
text:
4 Four formulations of classical mechanics
Five slides from 10 September 2026. The post caption is the readable source; the slides drop spaces.

Classical mechanics can be expressed through several equivalent mathematical formulations. Each predicts the same physical trajectories when its assumptions apply and the system is modelled consistently—but each emphasizes a different structure.
Newtonian mechanics begins with forces: \(\sum \mathbf F = m\ddot{\mathbf r}\).
Lagrangian mechanics uses generalized coordinates, energy, and stationary action: \(L=T-V\), \(\frac{d}{dt}\bigl(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}\bigr)
-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=Q_i^{(\mathrm{nc})}\).
Hamiltonian mechanics replaces generalized velocities with canonical momenta and describes motion as phase-space flow: \(\dot q_i=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i}\), \(\dot p_i=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}\).
Hamilton–Jacobi mechanics encodes the dynamics in Hamilton’s principal function \(S(q,t)\): \(\frac{\partial S}{\partial t}
+H\bigl(q,\frac{\partial S}{\partial q},t\bigr)=0\).







Overview: Newtonian, Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, and Hamilton–Jacobi side by side.







Newtonian mechanics: forces determine acceleration; pendulum as a free-body problem.









Lagrangian mechanics: energy, action, and the Euler–Lagrange equation.







Hamiltonian mechanics: Legendre transform and flow in phase space.









Hamilton–Jacobi: one nonlinear PDE for a generating function.





Linearisation of a vector field is a linear-algebra job: the local picture is \(\dot x = Ax\).

title: Analysis
text: Analysis is the study of limits, and of the operations that survive them: derivatives, integrals, infinite sums. The three galleries below, from @eeanimation, are the introduction to this page: branches of the subject, the standard calculus theorems, then complex analysis in more detail.

title: Analysis
text:
1 Branches of mathematical analysis
Real analysis builds the foundations. Complex analysis studies functions of \(z = x+iy\). Functional analysis moves to infinite dimensions; harmonic analysis reads frequency; numerical and asymptotic analysis approximate; variational and nonlinear analysis handle extrema and \(F(x)=0\).

title: Analysis
text:
3 Complex analysis
A function \(f:\Omega\subset\mathbb C\to\mathbb C\) is holomorphic if it is complex-differentiable on an open set. That single requirement is much stronger than real differentiability in two variables: Cauchy–Riemann, power series, contour integrals, residues, conformal maps.

section: 4 Bridges to the rest of the site
text:
4 Bridges to the rest of the site

Linear ODEs with constant coefficients are solved by characteristic polynomials — that is linear algebra over \(\mathbb C\).
Generating functions and characteristic functions in probability are analytic objects first, probabilistic ones second.
Hamilton–Jacobi theory on the dynamics page is a first-order nonlinear PDE.
